title: The Measurement Problem: What Happens When We Look?
question: Why does a quantum system behave as a spread of possibilities until it's observed, and what actually counts as an 'observation'?
summary: Quantum mechanics predicts a superposition of outcomes right up until measurement, at which point one outcome becomes real. A century after the theory's founding, physicists still cannot agree on what a measurement physically is, or why it seems to change the rules.
content:
The equations of quantum mechanics are not in dispute. Schrödinger's equation says a system evolves smoothly, deterministically, and reversibly into a superposition of every possible outcome. Then, the moment someone measures it, the superposition vanishes and a single definite result appears, chosen at random according to precise probabilities. Two processes, two very different kinds of physics, glued together with no agreed account of where one stops and the other begins. This is the measurement problem, and it has resisted resolution since the 1920s.

The Trouble with "Observation"

Nothing in the mathematics singles out human consciousness, a laboratory instrument, or even a specific moment in time as special. A photon detector is itself made of atoms that obey Schrödinger's equation, so in principle the detector plus the photon should also evolve into superposition — a "detector that has and hasn't detected the photon," entangled with the particle rather than collapsing it. Yet we never see instruments in superposition; we see one needle position, one click. Something breaks the chain of entanglement at some scale, but the theory itself doesn't say where.

Copenhagen's Shortcut

The historically dominant answer, associated with Bohr and Heisenberg, simply declares a line: quantum rules govern microscopic systems, classical rules govern measuring devices, and crossing that line causes collapse. This works remarkably well as a recipe for calculating experimental predictions, which is why it became the default taught in physics courses. But treated as physics rather than procedure, it's unsatisfying — it never says what physically constitutes a measuring device, nor why the universe should have two separate rulebooks with a fuzzy, undefined border between them.

Competing Attempts at a Real Answer

Several serious proposals try to remove the seam entirely. The Many-Worlds interpretation denies collapse ever happens: every outcome occurs, each in a decohered branch of a universal wavefunction, and "observation" just means the observer becomes entangled with one branch among many that no longer interact. Pilot-wave (de Broglie–Bohm) theory keeps particles always in definite positions, guided by a real physical wave, so there's no collapse to explain — only ignorance of the particle's actual trajectory. Objective collapse models (like GRW) go the opposite direction, proposing collapse is a real, tiny, constantly occurring physical process, occurring more often as systems get larger, which would in principle be experimentally detectable given a sensitive enough setup. Each removes the mystery at the cost of adding either unobservable parallel worlds, a hidden guiding field, or new physics beyond the standard Schrödinger equation.

What Decoherence Actually Explains, and Doesn't

Modern physics has made real progress on one piece of the puzzle: decoherence explains, using ordinary quantum mechanics, why superpositions of macroscopic objects become for all practical purposes unobservable almost instantly, since any interaction with a surrounding environment (air molecules, photons, thermal noise) rapidly entangles the system with vastly many uncontrolled degrees of freedom. This is why you never see a cat in superposition. But decoherence explains why we never see interference between branches — it does not explain why only one branch becomes "the" outcome we experience, rather than all of them continuing to exist unobserved. That residual question is exactly where the interpretations above still disagree.

perspectives.title: Copenhagen / Operational Physics
perspectives.description: Treats the measurement postulate as a working rule that correctly predicts experiments, and is skeptical that physics owes a deeper metaphysical story beyond that.

perspectives.title: Many-Worlds
perspectives.description: Argues collapse is an illusion produced by decoherence and an observer's inability to perceive branches other than their own, preserving a single, always-deterministic equation for the whole universe.

perspectives.title: Pilot-Wave Theory
perspectives.description: Restores definite particle trajectories at all times, trading the mystery of collapse for a nonlocal guiding wave that instantaneously coordinates distant particles.

perspectives.title: Objective Collapse Theories
perspectives.description: Proposes collapse is a real, spontaneous physical process with its own dynamics, testable in principle by looking for tiny deviations from standard quantum predictions in large, isolated systems.

perspectives.title: Quantum Information Theory
perspectives.description: Reframes the wavefunction itself as encoding an observer's knowledge or betting odds rather than physical reality (QBism), dissolving the problem by denying the wavefunction ever needed to 'really' collapse.

openQuestions: Is there any physically meaningful line between a 'quantum system' and a 'measuring device,' or is the distinction purely a matter of scale and complexity?
Could objective collapse models ever be confirmed or ruled out experimentally, given how small their predicted deviations from standard quantum mechanics are?
If Many-Worlds is correct, what physical meaning do probabilities even have, if every outcome occurs somewhere?
Does the measurement problem reflect an incompleteness in quantum theory itself, or a limitation in what any purely mathematical description of the universe could ever tell us about experience?
